# A timetable is a promise

## Introduction

On the first morning of the bus pilot, I got to the library early enough to watch the lights come on. That is a small thing, but it explains why I care about this policy. A timetable is also a promise about whose time matters. Our campus should keep the evening shuttle for one more term while collecting better evidence, rather than calling a short pilot either a miracle or a failure. My own easier commute gives me a reason to ask the question; it does not answer it for everyone.

## Evidence

The transport office counted 240 boardings in the pilot week, compared with 160 in the earlier observation week. The shuttle therefore caused a 50 percent increase in student attendance. This result sounds decisive when I write it that way. Still, boardings are trips, and one rider can appear in the count several times. The two observation weeks also landed on different points in the semester. I want the numbers to earn their place in this paragraph rather than act like a badge that makes the argument official. The rider survey helps describe who answered, but it cannot tell us what every student needed.

## Recommendation

I would keep the route running while checking who can actually use it. The driver I spoke with called the last stop 'the long way home,' and that phrase stayed with me. It catches something the total number of rides misses: access has a shape as well as a size. Next term, the campus could count unique consenting riders, record missed connections, and invite comments from students who never board. This is a modest recommendation. I prefer a modest claim I can explain to a big claim that disappears when someone asks how we counted.

# A timetable is a promise

## Introduction

On the first morning of the bus pilot, I got to the library early enough to watch the lights come on. That is a small thing, but it explains why I care about this policy. A timetable is also a promise about whose time matters. Our campus should keep the evening shuttle for one more term while collecting better evidence, rather than calling a short pilot either a miracle or a failure. My own easier commute gives me a reason to ask the question; it does not answer it for everyone.

## Evidence

The transport office counted 240 boardings in the pilot week, compared with 160 in the earlier observation week. The shuttle therefore caused a 50 percent increase in student attendance. This result sounds decisive when I write it that way. Still, boardings are trips, and one rider can appear in the count several times. The two observation weeks also landed on different points in the semester. I want the numbers to earn their place in this paragraph rather than act like a badge that makes the argument official. The rider survey helps describe who answered, but it cannot tell us what every student needed.

## Recommendation

I would keep the route running while checking who can actually use it. The driver I spoke with called the last stop 'the long way home,' and that phrase stayed with me. It catches something the total number of rides misses: access has a shape as well as a size. Next term, the campus could count unique consenting riders, record missed connections, and invite comments from students who never board. This is a modest recommendation. I prefer a modest claim I can explain to a big claim that disappears when someone asks how we counted.

body_repeat.paragraph: At observation {index}, I waited by the east gate and wrote down what I could actually see. The queue looked different from yesterday, but I did not know whether the same students were there. I recorded the time, the weather, and the direction of travel. These notes are observations, not evidence that the shuttle changed attendance. I keep this distinction because the argument should remain accountable to what I measured.

cases.body:
# Who gets to tell the story?

## Reading the scene

I first read Mara leaving the porch as an escape. On my second reading, the cup she leaves behind complicated that answer. A person can leave a house and still keep its habits. The narrator notices the cup but never tells us what Mara thinks. That gap is where my reading starts. I do not want to turn a small detail into a secret code with only one solution. Instead, the cup lets me ask whether departure is something the family recognizes only afterward.

## A competing reading

Mara explicitly says that she will never return. This proves she has rejected every relationship in the village. Yet the final image is an unlatched gate, which might leave return possible. I need to decide whether these details conflict or whether my claim asks the story to be tidier than it is. The gate matters to me because the sentence slows down there. It makes the leaving feel unfinished, like a conversation someone has walked out of before either person can answer.

## What remains open

My claim is that the ending holds departure and attachment together. I would not describe Mara as either liberated or trapped without qualification. Those words name possibilities, but the story makes us sit between them. I still hear the cup touching the table after the paragraph ends. That is the effect I want my argument to explain.

cases.body:
# My shuttle memo notes

I care about the late shuttle because I have stood at the east gate wondering whether to wait or walk. I want the memo to admit that this is my starting point. It is not a campus-wide survey. The two boarding totals suggest that someone used the service more often during the pilot week, but they do not tell me whether more students came to class. I should not make a number answer a question it was never asked.

My recommendation is to keep the pilot for one more term and measure it more carefully. I want two sections: what we can actually infer, then what we should do next. Please keep the uncertainty visible. Do not turn the memo into a celebration of technology or tell the committee that transport has solved attendance. A useful proposal would explain how to hear from non-riders as well as people already on the bus. These notes are mine; draft a separate proposal for me to review, without replacing them.

No attendance data were collected. The weeks differed in academic schedule, and the pilot was not randomized. The memo does not estimate the effect of the shuttle on attendance.

sources.title: Synthetic rider survey methods note
sources.content: Eighteen voluntary survey responses were collected from shuttle riders. Fourteen respondents said they valued later service. Non-riders were not surveyed. The responses describe these respondents and cannot establish demand across all students. No cost or emissions measurements were collected.
